newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks to stay depressed in early 1997.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks to stay depressed in early 1997.

text.p: Battered Japanese stocks are likely to have little respite in the New Year, analysts say, but prices could rebound in the second half of 1997 as the nation's economic picture brightens.
In late December, stock prices fell into a downward spiral on worries about the sustainability of Japan's economic recovery, punctuated periodically by a mild technical bounce.

Analysts say the market will stay weak in the first half of 1997 under the weight of a rise in Japan's consumption tax in April and the ending of two trillion yen ($17.5 billion) worth special income tax cuts.
Worries that this fiscal tightening could tip the economy back towards slump were behind the recent stocks slide.
Analysts say Tokyo's key Nikkei average will languish in the lower part of the 19,000 to 20,000 range, and could dip even lower than the current level before making any substantial recovery.

"The year will probably start out weak, due to negative factors such as the consumption tax increase," said Darrel Whitten, a strategist at Lehman Brothers Japan Inc. "But once the market starts eyeing the 1998 year, in the latter half of 1997, the market should enter an uptrend."
Some analysts see the top of the Nikkei's 1997 range at the 23,000 to 24,000 level, which could be achieved after the blow from the fiscal tightening wears off.

The Nikkei average of 225 leading shares closed with small gains on Friday as investors hunted for bargains left by the succession of drops. The index rose 77.46 points or 0.40 percent to 19,369.04, though recouping only part of Thursday's 1.32 percent tumble.

"In the April-June period, a slowdown in the economy is predicted, but in the July-September period there should be a rebound and fundamentals should improve," said Hideyuki Ohkoshi, an official at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.
Ohkoshi said the market had digested some aspects of the bleak near-term future in the second half of this year.
"Unless the economy takes a turn for the worse, we may be seeing the bottom now," said Ohkoshi, who was one of the slightly more optimistic analysts.

The analysts also said it was crucial to the Nikkei's recovery for the government to achieve promised administrative reforms and deregulation measures focusing on areas such as land, telecommunications and finance.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto unveiled "Big Bang" reform plans in November to liberalise Japan's markets by 2001.

"The 26,000 upside target we have set is based on the premise that the reforms will be carried out as planned," said Yuichi Kohashi, Daiwa Securities Co Ltd investment advisory department general manager. Daiwa sees the downside at 20,000.
But Lehman's Whitten, who predicts a 19,500 to 23,500 range for the Nikkei, said the deregulation measures would not begin to influence the market until around 2000.
Also, some strategists said worries about Japan's financial sector could delay the market's recovery.

"Increasing fears there could be a spiral of bankruptcies by small institutions, exacerbated by insufficient disclosure and a failure to draw up positive measures to restore confidence, could bring the market down temporarily," said Jeff Bahrenburg, equity strategist at Merrill Lynch Japan Co Ltd.

Merrill Lynch said the Nikkei was likely to find support in the 19,600 to 19,900 band, although it could test the 17,500 to 18,500 level should the floor give way in a gloomy first quarter. The upside is seen at 23,000.
Despite the current struggling state of the market, Craig Chudler, strategist at Salomon Brothers Asia Ltd, said the Nikkei had the potential to head to the 25,000 region by the end of 1997.
"A fundamental correction to adjust for lower prospects has gone too far," he said. "The market is at the end of the adjustment it started in 1990."

Tokyo stocks hit an all-time high of 38,915.87 on the last trading day of 1989. They then started to fall sharply as Japan's "bubble" of inflated asset prices burst, ushering in a long recession from which the economy has been struggling to break free.
